n: In this lecture we talk about agricultural chemicals, that is, pesticides. According to the outline, we review their classification, use and toxicological significance. The main groups: organophosphorus and organochlorine compounds and carbamic acid derivatives. In addition, we study their isolation from specimens and the general and specific methods of analysis, including GLC and HPLC.

What is a pesticide? Poisonous chemical compounds used in agriculture are called pesticides. The word is Latin: pestis means plague, and cido means killing. Pesticides are used against pests, for defoliation before harvest, against insects, and to influence plant growth.

t: Hazard of pesticides and residual amount
n: On the hazard of pesticides. If used incorrectly, pesticide residues poison air, soil and water and enter food and fodder. All poisonous chemicals are to some degree poisonous to humans as well. For this reason the expression “residual amount of pesticides” is used, and this amount must be below the permissible level.

Pesticides are divided into types by purpose. Acaricides are used against mites, insecticides against insects. Herbicides are used to destroy weeds. In the malaka lecture, fungicides are described as substances used against harmful fungi; TMTD, thiram and zineb are given as examples.

By toxicity, pesticides are divided into 4 groups according to their action through the gastrointestinal tract; this is determined in rats. The indicator is LD50, in mg/kg. In the highly toxic group the LD50 is 50 mg/kg. In the very toxic group 50-200, in the moderately toxic group 200-1000. In the slightly toxic group the LD50 is above 1000 mg/kg.

Chemically, pesticides are divided into three major classes. Inorganic compounds are salts and complex substances containing copper and arsenic. Organic pesticides consist of synthesised and natural compounds. Organometallic pesticides are organic compounds containing mercury and other metals.

Synthetic organic pesticides are divided into four groups. Organophosphorus compounds, OPCs: metaphos, mercaptophos, carbophos, phosalone, chlorophos; medicinal forms benzotef, nibufen, imifos. Synthetic pyrethroids: cypermethrin, decis, danitol, karate, sumi-alpha. Derivatives of carbamic and thiocarbonic acids: sevin, thiram, zineb, TMTD. Halogen-containing hydrocarbons: DDT, hexachlorane, heptachlor.

Let us recall the remaining groups too. Amine derivatives include diquat and paraquat. Derivatives of ketones, alcohols, nitrophenols and simple ethers include dinitro-ortho-cresol. Compounds from plants are anabasine and nicotine.

The toxicological significance of organophosphorus compounds is explained by the fact that they are poisonous and are widely used in agriculture in large amounts. For example, chlorophos is used in caring for agricultural plants as an insecticide and acaricide; at home it is also used against flies. In the DVSSM complex the main use of chlorophos is given in the same way.

Examples of poisoning cases. In the literature it is described that a woman who drank a 1.5% solution of carbophos died. When a four-year-old child drank water from a glass with traces of thiophos, death occurred. OPC can also be absorbed through the skin and lead to death: a child who played with a container emptied of thiophos died after 30 minutes.

t: Mechanism of action of OPC: cholinesterase
n: The poisonous action of OPC is explained by their ability to inhibit the activity of the enzyme cholinesterase. OPC belong to the group of substances with anticholinesterase action. As a result cholinesterase is blocked, hydrolysis of the mediator acetylcholine is impaired, and it accumulates excessively in nerve cells. In this way the neurotoxic effect arises.

Signs of OPC poisoning. Headache, nausea, vomiting, abdominal pain, profuse salivation and sweating are observed. The pupil constricts, the tips of the hands and feet tremble, and a feeling of fear appears. Blood pressure first rises and then falls; death occurs from respiratory arrest. When the corpse is opened, a foul smell of mercaptan may be noticed in the gastrointestinal tract; the only pathological-anatomical sign is haemorrhages into internal organs.

The significance of organochlorine compounds is explained by their wide use in agriculture as insecticides; they are used as dusts or as solutions in oil. Oil solutions are especially poisonous: they are absorbed quickly, well taken up by the kidneys, adipose tissue and bone marrow, and slowly excreted. Organochlorine substances are very stable: in natural conditions they remain unchanged for a long time and accumulate in soil and groundwater.

Let us give an example of the metabolism of organochlorine substances. From DDT, the less toxic dichlorodiphenylacetic acid is formed. From heptachlor, the oxidation product heptachlor epoxide is formed, an even more potent poison. Signs: headache, weakness, trembling of the hands and feet, salivation, startling. Death occurs from failure of the central nervous and cardiovascular systems. For chemical examination, internal organs of the corpse, animals and food products are taken; the examination is carried out on the instruction of the investigator.

t: Isolation of OPC from a biological specimen
n: The procedure for isolating OPC from a biological specimen. The specimen is finely minced, and hydrochloric or sulphuric acid is added until the required medium is obtained. Then it is soaked with an organic solvent and left for one hour at room temperature; soaking is repeated 2-3 more times. The combined solvent is evaporated with a vacuum pump or on a water bath, and the residue is dissolved in alcohol. Alternative method: extraction with hexane in the presence of anhydrous sodium sulphate.

Fat must be removed, because fat and fat-like substances also pass into the organic solvent layer, especially from the gastrointestinal tract, kidneys and liver. After the solvent is removed, the residue is mixed with a small amount of acetone and cooled in a freezer. The fat solidifies and rises to the surface, while the OPC passes into the acetone layer; the process is repeated several times. For additional clean-up, a column with sorbent and thin-layer chromatography are used.

The general reaction is the phosphomolybdenum blue reaction. Part of the extract is evaporated to dryness, and the residue is mineralised with sulphuric and nitric acids. The mineralisate gives a yellow colour with ammonium molybdate; under the action of benzidine or ascorbic acid, a stable blue complex forms. The method is highly sensitive, but all phosphorus-containing substances give this reaction, so a negative result is significant.

The first method based on anticholinesterase action is based on determining unhydrolysed acetylcholine as a result of blocking of the enzyme by OPC. The amount of accumulated acetylcholine is directly proportional to the amount of OPC. The source of the enzyme is blood serum. When hydroxylamine and iron (III) chloride are added, acetylcholine gives the red iron complex of acetohydroxamic acid.

The indicator method is based on a change in indicator colour under the action of acetic acid formed by hydrolysis of excess acetylcholine. The indicator is a weakly alkaline solution of bromothymol blue, the enzyme source is horse blood serum; the colour changes from blue to yellow. The duration of the colour change must be 13 minutes. A decrease in the enzyme of 10% indicates the presence of OPC.

There are substances that interfere with this method. Substances with anticholinesterase action interfere: sevin, proserin, galantamine, alcohol, protein breakdown products. For this reason this reaction too is significant for chemical-toxicological analysis only when negative. To determine the amount, phosphomolybdenum blue, the iron salt of acetohydroxamic acid, that is, the photometric method, or UV spectrophotometry is used.

The general scheme of OPC analysis. First the general reaction for phosphorus, that is, phosphomolybdenum blue, is carried out, then methods based on anticholinesterase action are used. Then TLC is performed: 4 spots are applied to the start line, each is sprayed with a different reagent; Rf and colour are compared. According to the result, for analysis directed at a particular substance, 100 g of specimen is isolated by the appropriate method.

On the OPC that must be analysed. According to Order No. 551 of the Ministry of Health, the number of OPC that must be analysed is 10. The list: carbophos, metaphos, methylethylthiophos, methylnitrophos, trichlorometaphos-3, phosphamide, methylmercaptophos, phthalophos, phosalone, butiphos. In the DVSSM complex the same list is given.

t: TLC: determining the nature of OPC
n: Determining the nature of OPC by TLC. Four spots from the extract are applied to the start line; the chamber is filled with chloroform saturated with water. The zone of each spot is sprayed with a different reagent: bromophenol blue and acetic acid, sodium hydroxide, Dragendorff reagent, resorcinol in alkali. If in the bromophenol blue zone a blue spot appears on a yellow background, this proves that the substance is a derivative of thio- and dithiophosphoric acid.

We interpret the TLC results. Sulphur-containing preparations with a para-nitrophenol residue, that is, metaphos, methylnitrophos and methylethylthiophos, give a yellow colour in alkali. Octamethyl and chlorophos are not detected with bromophenol blue. Dragendorff reagent gives a brown spot with octamethyl and some nitrogen-containing substances, that is, phosalone, phthalophos, phosphamide. Chlorophos forms a red spot with resorcinol. After Rf and colour are determined, for analysis directed at a particular substance, 100 g of specimen is isolated by the appropriate method.

There are additional reactions for chlorophos and carbophos. Chlorophos with an alcoholic solution of acetone and alkali gives pink, then red and flame colour; with 2,4-dinitrophenylhydrazine a blue or blue-violet colour forms. The metabolites of chlorophos, dichlorvos and dichloroacetaldehyde, are identified by TLC; system chloroform-ether-liquid paraffin 17:2:1. For carbophos, the yellow-lemon copper complex of dimethoxydithiophosphoric acid is obtained; the reaction with iodine monochloride is positive.

t: Isolation of OPC: pH and solvent (malaka)
n: The malaka lecture gives a table of isolation medium and solvent for certain OPC. Carbophos is isolated at pH 1 with benzene. Chlorophos at pH 2 with ether. Phosalone at pH 7 with ether. Butiphos is also isolated at pH 7 with ether.

On phosalone. In pure form it is a crystalline substance with a garlic smell, soluble in alcohol and organic solvents; melting point 47-48 °C. It is used as a 35% emulsion concentrate and an 80% powder. The LD50 for rats is 108 mg/kg; the permissible content in air is 0.5 mg/m3. Phosalone is not volatile; it is stable in an acidic medium, rapidly hydrolysed in an alkaline one, and passes into the blood through the skin.

Microcrystalline reactions are used to confirm phosalone. With an alcoholic solution of silver nitrate, colourless needle-shaped crystals form; detection limit 0.5 µg. An alcoholic solution of copper nitrate gives bluish needle-shaped crystals, limit 2 µg; iodine monochloride gives brown needle-shaped microcrystals, also 2 µg. Mercury (II) chloride or bromide forms spherulites, limit 4 µg. In TLC, chloroform saturated with water and bromophenol blue are used, Rf 0.65-0.67, a blue spot on a yellow background; UV spectrophotometry is also used.

Isolation of sevin. Sevin, a carbamic acid derivative, is isolated from biological material as follows: the specimen is crushed and soaked three times for one hour with benzene. The benzene layers are combined and evaporated; the residue is extracted with a mixture of NH4Cl, H3PO4 and acetone. The acetone is evaporated, and the residue is extracted with chloroform. Together with sevin, its metabolite naphthol also passes into the chloroform.

For sevin, the TLC system is chloroform, benzene and acetone, ratio 7:2:1; the spots are sprayed with sodium cuprobromide. Naphthol gives an ink-violet spot with Rf 0.45. With diazotised sulfanilic acid, sevin gives a red spot with Rf 0.8. The malaka lecture gives yellow microcrystals with picric acid, and with HgCl2 microcrystals of hexagonal or prismatic shape.

TMTD, that is, tetramethylthiuram disulphide, is a derivative of carbamic and thiocarbonic acid mentioned as a fungicide. For confirmation, star-shaped flame-coloured microcrystals are obtained with 0.2 N iodine monochloride. In TLC the system toluene, acetone and hexane 1:1:1 is used; with bromophenol reagent a blue spot forms on a yellow background with Rf 0.68.

Properties of hexachlorocyclohexane, abbreviated HCH. It is synthesised by photochemical chlorination of benzene; a mixture of 8 stereoisomers, a bluish substance with a musty smell and a suffocating odour. The insecticide containing 99-100% of the gamma isomer is called lindane. It is poorly soluble in water, readily soluble in alcohol and ether, and distils with steam. The melting point of the isomer is 112.8 °C.

Toxicological significance of HCH. It acts as an insecticide and fumigant through contact and the gastrointestinal tract; it is also used for dressing grain seeds. The LD50 for rats is 400 mg/kg; for the gamma isomer 200 mg/kg. In poisoning, excitation, slowing of respiration, impaired movement, convulsions and trembling in the legs are observed, and hormone activity is disrupted. In chronic poisoning the substance accumulates and is slowly eliminated from the body.

t: HCH: isolation and reaction with alkali
n: HCH is isolated by the Rubtsov method. By steam distillation, 300 ml of distillate is obtained and extracted three times with ether. In the alternative method the specimen is soaked with ether and the extract is passed through a column of activated charcoal. With an alcoholic solution of alkali, chlorine is converted to chloride anion and determined with silver nitrate in nitric acid; three molecules of HCl are formed.

Identity reactions for HCH. With alcohol and metallic sodium all the chlorine is released; the amounts of white precipitates in the two reactions should differ in a ratio of about 1:2. When converted to the nitro compound, the trinitrobenzene formed gives a blue-violet colour with methyl alcohol alcoholate; sensitivity 0.05 mg. TLC from blood: with n-hexane and silica gel Rf 0.19; on an aluminium oxide plate Rf 0.34, with silver ammonia complex, 10-15 minutes UV. Isomers and metabolites are determined by GLC, GC-MS and HPLC.

General procedure for isolation from blood and urine. For blood: 5 ml of sample is brought to pH 8-9, 2 ml of saturated NaCl and 10 ml of organic solvent are added; centrifuged for 5 minutes, and the extraction is repeated 2 times. For urine: 25 ml of sample and 3 g of NaCl, pH 8-9, that is, 0.1 M NaOH; extracted 3 times, with 30, 20 and 20 ml of organic solvent. The dry residue is examined by TLC, HPLC and UV spectrometry.

t: Isolation from a biological specimen and summary
n: Isolation from a biological specimen. 10 g of biological specimen is crushed, mixed with 1-3 ml of water, and brought to pH 9-9.5, that is, with 0.1 M NaOH. 15 ml of organic solvent and 5 ml of saturated NaCl are added and left for 1 hour on a shaker; extraction is repeated twice more. The combined extract is passed through sodium sulphate and evaporated on a rotary vacuum evaporator. The residue is examined by TLC, UV or HPLC.

We compare the three groups. OPC inhibit the enzyme cholinesterase; the LD50 of phosalone is 108 mg/kg, in rats. Organochlorine substances are very stable and slowly eliminated from the body; for HCH the γ-isomer has an LD50 of 200 mg/kg. Sevin, that is, a carbamic acid derivative, is isolated with benzene; its metabolite naphthol also passes into the chloroform.

To conclude. Pesticides are studied by chemical structure: OPC, organochlorine compounds, carbamic acid derivatives and others. OPC inhibit cholinesterase; in analysis, phosphomolybdenum blue, anticholinesterase methods and TLC, that is, 4 spots and 4 reagents, are used. Organochlorine substances are stable and slowly eliminated; for HCH, alkali, sodium, the nitro compound, TLC and GLC, HPLC, GC-MS are used. Sevin is isolated with benzene, and in TLC naphthol gives Rf 0.45 and sevin Rf 0.8.
